evidence.notes: The final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with a following vowel sound and is pronounced [z], as stated in the batch source text. Confidence high.
On can mean we, but the verb always stays in the third person singular; this is the neutral impersonal use described in the context. Confidence high.
Savoir plus infinitive means to know how to do something; the related_examples give exactly Elle sait jouer du piano. Confidence high.

patches.value: ils parlent [il paʁl] (la terminaison -ent est muette)

evidence.notes: The -e, -es and -ent endings of regular -er verbs are silent, so ils parlent sounds identical to il parle; the source text states these endings are all silent. Confidence high.
Vieux becomes vieil before a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel or mute h; the context names vieux to vieil among the special forms. Confidence high.
Vous is the correct address form for a stranger or someone you do not know well, as stated in the source text. Confidence high.

entity_key.title: Using present tense with depuis vs English

patches.value: J'habite à Paris depuis cinq ans.

evidence.notes: French uses the present tense with depuis for an action that started in the past and continues, where English uses the past tense or present perfect. Context confirms this contrast. Confidence high.
